CHAPTER XCVII

A priest is never more thoroughly a priest than in the chamber of death,
Gerard did the last offices of the Church for the departed, just as
he should have done them for his smallest parishioner. He did this
mechanically, then sat down stupefied by the sudden and tremendous blow,
and not yet realizing the pangs of bereavement. Then in a transport of
religious enthusiasm he kneeled and thanked Heaven for her Christian
end.

And then all his thought was to take her away from strangers, and lay
her in his own churchyard. That very evening a covered cart with one
horse started for Gouda, and in it was a coffin, and a broken-hearted
man lying with his arms and chin resting on it.

The mourner's short-lived energy had exhausted itself in the necessary
preparations, and now he lay crushed, clinging to the cold lead that
held her.

The man of whom the cart was hired walked by the horse's head and did
not speak to him, and when he baited the horse spoke but in a whisper
respecting that mute agony. But when he stopped for the night, he and
the landlord made a well-meaning attempt to get the mourner away to take
some rest and food. But Gerard repulsed them, and when they persisted,
almost snarled at them, like a faithful dog, and clung to the cold lead
all night. So then they drew a cloak over him, and left him in peace.

And at noon the sorrowful cart came up to the manse, and there were
full a score of parishioners collected with one little paltry trouble or
another. They had missed the parson already. And when they saw what it
was, and saw their healer so stricken down, they raised a loud wail of
grief, and it roused him from his lethargy of woe, and he saw where he
was, and their faces, and tried to speak to them, “Oh, my children! my
children!” he cried; but choked with anguish, could say no more.

Yet the next day, spite of all remonstrances, he buried her himself,
and read the service with a voice that only trembled now and then, Many
tears fell upon her grave. And when the service ended he stayed there
standing like a statue, and the people left the churchyard out of
respect.

He stood like one in a dream till the sexton, who was, as most men are,
a fool, began to fill in the grave without giving him due warning.

But at the sound of earth falling on her Gerard uttered a piercing
scream.

The sexton forbore.

Gerard staggered and put his hand to his breast. The sexton supported
him, and called for help.

Jorian Ketel, who lingered near mourning his benefactress, ran into the
churchyard, and the two supported Gerard into the manse.

“Ah, Jorian! good Jorian!” said he, “something snapped within me; I
felt it, and I heard it; here, Jorian, here;” and he put his hand to his
breast.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

To truly comprehend the sanctity of the final rites, one must witness them performed not merely as duty, but as a desperate anchor against the void of mortality. In the chamber of death, Gerard was never more fully a priest than when he tended the departing soul of his beloved, executing the last offices of the Church with the same mechanical precision he would have applied to the smallest parishioner. Yet, once the rituals concluded, the machinery of faith ground to a halt. He sat, stupefied by the sudden, tremendous blow, paralyzed by a grief he had not yet recognized as such. Only then, in a transport of religious fervor born of sheer necessity, did he kneel to thank Heaven for her Christian end. His singular, consuming thought became immediate extraction: to remove her from the gaze of strangers and inter her within the sacred soil of his own churchyard.

That very evening, a covered cart drawn by a single horse departed for Gouda, carrying a coffin and a broken-hearted man whose arms and chin rested upon the cold wood. The mourner's short-lived energy had been entirely expended in the arduous preparations; now, he lay crushed, clinging to the leaden box that held her remains. The driver, a silent figure of routine, walked beside the horse's head, offering no comfort, speaking only in whispers when he baited the animal, respectful of the mute agony radiating from the passenger. When they halted for the night, the landlord and the driver made a well-meaning attempt to coax the mourner away for rest and sustenance. But Gerard repulsed them, snarling like a faithful dog guarding its burden, refusing to be parted from the cold lead even as sleep claimed him. They were forced to draw a cloak over him and leave him in peace.

At noon the following day, the sorrowful cart arrived at the manse, greeted by a score of parishioners gathered with their trivial domestic troubles momentarily suspended. They had missed the parson already, sensing a shift in the spiritual atmosphere. Upon seeing the scene—their healer so utterly stricken—they raised a loud wail of grief. This collective sound pierced the lethargy of his woe, rousing him from his stupor. He looked around, recognizing the familiar faces, and tried to speak to them, crying out, "Oh, my children! My children!" but choked on the rawness of his anguish, unable to form further words.

Yet, despite all remonstrances, the next day he buried her himself. He read the service with a voice that trembled only occasionally, many tears falling upon the fresh earth of her grave. When the service ended, he remained standing like a statue amidst the silent congregation, who left the churchyard out of profound respect. He stood thus, lost in a waking dream, until the sexton—a man of common sense and limited wisdom—began to fill in the grave without due warning. At the sound of earth falling upon her, Gerard uttered a piercing scream. The sexton forbore from finishing his work. Gerard staggered, clutching his breast, and the sexton supported him, calling loudly for aid. Jorian Ketel, who had lingered nearby mourning his benefactress, ran into the churchyard. Together, the two men supported the shattered priest back to the manse. "Ah, Jorian! Good Jorian!" he gasped, his voice breaking. "Something snapped within me; I felt it, and I heard it; here, Jorian, here;" and he pressed his hand firmly against his heart.
